transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

I’m constantly hung up on how my face looks on camera and in person, and it’s making me avoid people and things I used to enjoy. It's gotten to the point where I'm dodging social outings and work meetings because I'm just so self-conscious. A close friend noticed how much I was pulling back and suggested I come in to talk to someone.
Is your avoidance of social situations entirely due to concerns about how your face looks, or do you also worry about being judged for your actions, words, or showing signs of nervousness?

Yes, it's entirely because of how my face looks, specifically my crooked jaw and the scar on my cheek. I don't really worry about what I say, how I act, or showing signs of nervousness. My anxiety is purely about people judging those physical features.
How long have you been experiencing these intense concerns about your jaw and scar?

They first started as a quiet, background worry back in my late teens after a sports injury left me with the scar and a slightly uneven jaw. However, it got much worse during the pandemic when my school shifted to online teaching and I had to look at my own image on camera for hours every day.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time checking your face in mirrors, trying to hide your jaw or scar, or comparing your appearance to others?

Yes, I constantly check my face using my phone camera, zooming in on my scar and jaw, and taking dozens of selfies at night just to delete them. I also try to hide how I look by fiddling with my beard, tilting my head on Zoom, and constantly comparing myself to my colleagues and influencers online. It's incredibly exhausting and really hard to stop.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of intense preoccupation with perceived physical flaws (a crooked jaw and a scar), repetitive behaviors (frequent camera checking, grooming, comparing), and significant social/occupational avoidance confirm a diagnosis of Body Dysmorphic Disorder, which is classified under F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder/Dysmorphophobia) in ICD-10. Social phobia (F40.1) has been ruled out as the anxiety is strictly related to appearance rather than fear of negative evaluation of behavior or nervousness. No further questioning is required.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a severe preoccupation with perceived defects in their physical appearance (a crooked jaw and a scar on the cheek) which are either non-existent or only slight to others. This preoccupation causes significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning, leading to avoidance of social outings and work meetings. The patient engages in time-consuming repetitive behaviors (mirror/camera checking, taking/deleting selfies, camouflaging with a beard and head positioning, and comparing appearance with others). Social phobia (F40.1) was considered but ruled out because the patient's social anxiety and avoidance are driven purely by concerns about their physical features rather than fear of negative evaluation regarding their actions, words, or trembling.
